title: When do you use an IAM Role instead of an IAM User (temporary credentials via STS, cross-account access, EC2/Lambda assuming a role) — and why should application code never embed long-lived access keys?
shortTitle: IAM Role versus IAM User and Why Code Must Never Embed Long-Lived Keys

s1_definition.profdef: You use an IAM Role whenever an identity should receive temporary, automatically-rotated credentials rather than permanent keys. The canonical cases are a compute resource such as EC2 or Lambda that needs to call AWS services, cross-account access where a principal in one account assumes a Role in another, and any federated or short-lived access. STS (Security Token Service) issues the temporary credentials when a Role is assumed, and they expire after a set duration. Application code must never embed long-lived access keys because such keys do not expire, can leak through source control or logs, and give an attacker durable access until a human manually rotates them.
s1_definition.analogy: An IAM User's access key is like giving a contractor a permanent master key to National Bank of India that never stops working — if he loses it, a thief can enter the vault forever. An IAM Role is like a temporary visitor badge printed at the front desk that stops working after one hour. If the badge is dropped in the car park, it is already useless. So for machines and contractors we always hand out the expiring badge, never the permanent master key.
s1_definition.oneliner: Use a Role for machines, cross-account, and anything temporary, because it hands out expiring credentials, while an embedded long-lived key is a secret that never expires and never should exist in code.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** You use an IAM Role whenever an identity should receive temporary, automatically-rotated credentials rather than permanent keys. The canonical cases are a compute resource such as EC2 or Lambda that needs to call AWS services, cross-account access where a principal in one account assumes a Role in another, and any federated or short-lived access. STS (Security Token Service) issues the temporary credentials when a Role is assumed, and they expire after a set duration. Application code must never embed long-lived access keys because such keys do not expire, can leak through source control or logs, and give an attacker durable access until a human manually rotates them.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** An IAM User's access key is like giving a contractor a permanent master key to National Bank of India that never stops working — if he loses it, a thief can enter the vault forever. An IAM Role is like a temporary visitor badge printed at the front desk that stops working after one hour. If the badge is dropped in the car park, it is already useless. So for machines and contractors we always hand out the expiring badge, never the permanent master key.

**One line to remember:** Use a Role for machines, cross-account, and anything temporary, because it hands out expiring credentials, while an embedded long-lived key is a secret that never expires and never should exist in code.

sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The settlement service runs on EC2 and must read a settlement file from S3. A junior engineer's first instinct is to paste an access key and secret into the code so it "just works." That key then lives in the repository history forever and is a standing breach waiting to happen. This is exactly what an IAM Role fixes: the EC2 instance assumes a Role and the credentials are temporary, so there is no secret in the code.

Problem 2 — A separate analytics account must read the same settlement data for reporting. Copying production keys into analytics would spread the secret across accounts. This is exactly what cross-account Role assumption fixes: analytics assumes a production Role and gets short-lived scoped credentials.

We will model a `CredentialProvider` that either returns a dangerous embedded key (the wrong way) or temporary credentials from a simulated STS (the right way), an `AssumeRoleService` that mints expiring tokens, and a demo that shows the token expiring. Classes: `TemporaryCredentials`, `AssumeRoleService`, `SettlementReader`.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a Role ARN for the settlement reader and a cross-account Role ARN for analytics.

Step 1 — The EC2-hosted service calls `assumeRole` with the settlement Role ARN and a one-hour time-to-live. The `AssumeRoleService` simulates STS and returns `TemporaryCredentials` with a session token and an expiry one hour in the future. No permanent key exists anywhere.

Step 2 — The `SettlementReader` is built with those temporary credentials. When it reads the file it first checks the credentials have not expired, then performs the read. Because the credentials are valid, the read succeeds.

Step 3 — The analytics account calls `assumeRole` with the production Role ARN and a thirty-minute time-to-live. It gets its own short-lived token scoped to production read access, without ever holding a production access key.

Step 4 — The demo logs a warning describing the wrong way: embedding a key like `AKIA...` in code. That key would never expire and would leak permanently, which is why it is forbidden.

```
2026-10-29 00:52:14 [INFO] Assumed Role, token expires at 2026-10-29T01:52:14Z
2026-10-29 00:52:14 [INFO] Read settlement file: contents-of-SETL-2026-10-29.csv
2026-10-29 00:52:14 [INFO] Cross-account token expires at 2026-10-29T01:22:14Z
2026-10-29 00:52:14 [WARNING] Embedding an access key in code (AKIA...) would never expire and leak forever
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  EC2 settlement service
    │ assumeRole(SettlementReaderRole, 1h)
    ▼
  STS ──→ TemporaryCredentials {sessionToken, expiry = now+1h}
    │
    ▼
  SettlementReader.read("SETL-2026-10-29.csv")
    │ expired? ── no ──→ S3 GetObject ──→ file contents
    │ expired? ── yes ─→ refresh via STS

  Analytics account ──assumeRole(ProdSettlementReadRole,30m)──→ STS
    │ cross-account trust policy allows analytics principal
    ▼
  Short-lived prod read token (scoped, 30 min)
```

```
                                   │ SettlementReader        │

  [ISSUED] ──1h──→ [EXPIRED] ──refresh──→ [ISSUED]

  Contract for read(key):
    Pre:  credentials not expired
    Post: returns file contents
    Throws: IllegalStateException if expired
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
I reach for an IAM Role instead of an IAM User whenever the identity is a machine, needs cross-account access, or should only have temporary access. The three classic cases are compute resources like EC2 and Lambda that call AWS services, cross-account access where a principal in one account assumes a Role in another, and federated users who log in through an identity provider. In all of these, STS issues temporary credentials when the Role is assumed, and those credentials expire, usually after an hour.

The reason this matters, especially in banking, comes down to blast radius. An IAM User access key is a permanent two-part secret that never expires on its own. The moment it lands in a Git commit, a Docker image layer, a log line, or a stack trace, it is compromised forever until a human notices and rotates it, and attackers scan public repositories for these strings within seconds. Temporary credentials from a Role cap the damage to the token's short lifetime, so even a leaked token is useless within the hour.

At National Bank of India our settlement service runs on EC2 with an instance profile that wraps a Role. The AWS SDK's default credential provider automatically fetches the temporary credentials from the instance metadata, uses them, and refreshes them before they expire, so we write no credential-handling code at all and there is simply no secret to leak. For reporting, a separate analytics account assumes a production Role whose trust policy names the analytics account, so analytics reads production settlement data with short-lived scoped credentials instead of us copying production keys across accounts.

So the rule I state plainly in an interview is that application code must never embed long-lived access keys, because a secret that never expires is a breach waiting to happen. For services we use Roles through instance profiles or execution roles, for cross-account we use trust policies and assume-role, and even for local development we use SSO or named profiles rather than keys in the code. One senior detail I mention is that when one Role assumes another, role chaining caps the session at one hour regardless of the configured maximum, which is a useful guardrail to know.

keyPoints: User: person. Group: collection of users. Role: temporary credentials
Principle of least privilege: grant minimum required access
